newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-COURT TO ACCEPT MAJORITY VERDICT IN UK SOCCER CASE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COURT TO ACCEPT MAJORITY VERDICT IN UK SOCCER CASE.

text.p: Jurors in Britain's soccer match-rigging trial were told on Friday the court would accept a majority verdict on the last remaining charge against goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar.
Zimbabwe-born Grobbelaar was alone in the dock after his three co-defendants walked free on Thursday.

He was cleared on Thursday of one charge of attempting to fix matches in England's Premier soccer league, but the jury was divided over a second charge that he accepted 2,000 pounds ($3,200) to influence the outcome of games.
Two other soccer stars, former Aston Villa striker John Fashanu and Dutch-born goalkeeper Hans Segers, were cleared in unanimous verdicts in Britain's most sensational soccer trial.
Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim was also unanimously found not guilty, leaving Grobbelaar, 39, the lone remaining defendant.

Judge Charles McCullough said that on the final charge against Grobbelaar he would accept a verdict on which at least 10 of the 11 jurors agreed. The jury of six men and five women in the nine-week old trial began its sixth day of deliberations on Friday.
The freed defendants were back in court on Friday, taking their seats in the public gallery to hear the verdict on Grobbelaar.
Dutch-born Segers said on Thursday after he was acquitted that he was ready to resume his career.

"Its been a nightmare for 2-1/2 years, but we got the verdict we deserved," said Segers, the 35-year-old former goalkeeper for Wimbledon. "Today is just an unbelievable day and it has been very emotional."
It was the second time the four had faced trial in the case. Another jury was dismissed earlier this year after failing to reach verdicts.
Fashanu, 33, who declined to testify during the court proceedings, said he was not bitter at having had to face two trials.
"Now all I want to do is get on with my beautiful wife and go back to my friends," he said.
The former Aston Villa and Wimbledon striker is now a popular television presenter and a highly successful businessman.
The four had all denied the allegations they were involved with an Asian gambling syndicate.

The prosecution had investigated huge cash sums the defendants deposited in their bank accounts and traced dozens of telephone calls they made to one another, but the jury concluded these were not evidence they had been rigging matches.
The case is reported to have cost millions of pounds and has shaken the image of British football.
The English Football Association announced after Thursday's verdicts that it was carrying out a detailed inquiry into the rules on betting and forecasting in the game.
The former Deputy Commissioner of London's Metropolitan Police, Sir John Smith, is leading the inquiry and is due to report back within three months.
